headline: Desheng Ma and Steven Zeltmann show that a 4D-STEM dataset is already a light-field photograph, so depth slices through a specimen fall out of one four-dimensional Fourier transform — over ten times faster once more than ten depths are wanted.

items.title: A 4D-STEM scan is a light-field photograph, and depth slices fall out of one FFT
items.dek: Desheng Ma and Steven Zeltmann at Cornell showed that a 4D-STEM dataset — the whole diffraction pattern a scanning transmission electron microscope records at every probe position — is mathematically a light-field photograph, so depth slices through a specimen are planes cut from one four-dimensional Fourier transform.
items.why_it_matters: Getting depth out of these datasets has meant registering and summing hundreds of shifted virtual images, once per depth, which is why almost nobody sweeps the whole thickness. Recasting the operation as slicing a single transform makes the cost nearly flat in the number of depths asked for, and it needs no extra electrons, because the measurement was already on disk.
items.background_md: An electron microscope records a projection: everything along the beam path collapses into one image, so a 30-nanometre film looks like a single layer. Depth is encoded anyway, because a converged probe is a cone — features above and below the focal crossover sweep in opposite directions as the probe scans, which is ordinary parallax. Recovering it has meant either tilting the specimen through many angles, which costs dose and time, or iterative phase retrieval, which costs compute and can fail to converge. That is why depth sectioning stays rare in practice.
items.deeper_md:
The paper's three framings are the content. Viewing the 4D data as angular slices turns it into a set of sinograms, and within the small-angle approximation tilt-corrected bright field (tcBF) is then exactly a non-iterative tomographic reconstruction. Mapping it instead onto plenoptic imaging gives the computational result: a depth section is a 2D slice through a single 4D FFT of the dataset, worth over 10× once more than about ten slices are wanted. Aberration-corrected bright field (acBF) additionally inverts the phase contrast transfer function, which removes the contrast rings tcBF leaves and flattens the response with depth.

Measured depth resolution on a twisted SrTiO₃ bilayer: knife-edge widths of 5.79 and 4.21 nm for one layer and 5.46 and 5.43 nm for the other, against a 4.52 nm limit from the contrast transfer envelope, with the two lattices separated at 19.5 and 26.7 nm. Three overlapping Pt grains were split across 21.7–26.7, 26.7–30.8 and 30.8–35.8 nm.

The limit is geometric and the authors state it: a 30 mrad convergence semi-angle gives only a 3.4° tilt range on any single axis, leaving a missing cone of 176.6° opening, so flat wide features have no axial resolution. The weak-phase assumption also fails in thick, heavy-element specimens, which is where iterative multislice ptychography still has to be used.

glossary.definition: Recording a full 2D diffraction pattern at each of the 2D probe positions in a scan, so the dataset has four dimensions and every detector pixel defines its own image of the sample.

Tilt-corrected bright field realigns the parallax-shifted virtual images before summing them; aberration-corrected bright field also undoes the phase contrast transfer function, removing the contrast rings tcBF leaves behind.
The unit of the electron probe's convergence semi-angle; 30 mrad is about 1.7°, and it sets both the lateral resolution and how much parallax is available to work with.
The band of spatial frequencies no finite tilt range or parallax measurement can reach, which is why axial resolution collapses for features that are wide and flat.

items.fab_angle: The demonstration samples are stacked oxide films and overlapping metal grains, which is the shape of almost every interesting failure in a bonded or 3D-stacked wafer. A non-iterative depth sweep from a dataset you already took is the version of this a shared-user TEM can actually run.

items.title: A solid immersion lens you deposit on the diamond instead of milling into it
items.dek: Michael Bar and co-workers at Leipzig built the light-collection lens for a nitrogen-vacancy centre — a single atom-scale emitter sitting inside diamond — by depositing yttria-stabilised zirconia on the surface at room temperature, rather than milling the lens into the diamond with an ion beam.
items.why_it_matters: A milled lens is a one-shot operation: the beam must locate the emitter first, and it removes crystal that cannot be put back, so a mis-aimed cut spoils that patch of diamond permanently. A deposited film can be stripped and retried and is patterned by ordinary photolithography, which moves the binding error from beam placement to mask alignment — a different and much cheaper tool.
items.background_md: Diamond's refractive index is 2.41, so light leaving a defect inside it is totally internally reflected at the flat top surface unless it arrives within about 25° of the normal, the critical angle for that index. That cone is most of the photon budget in single-emitter work, where optical spin readout contrast is set by how many photons you collect in a few hundred nanoseconds. A solid immersion lens fixes the geometry rather than the material: put a hemisphere centred on the emitter and every ray crosses the exit surface along a radius, so nothing refracts on the way out.
items.deeper_md:
The deposited oxide is not index-matched: the paper puts yttria-stabilised zirconia at n = 2.17 at 632 nm against 2.41 for diamond, so the lens is chosen for what can be grown rather than for a perfect match. Films go down at room temperature in 0.01 mbar of oxygen, 500,000 pulses at 20 Hz and 2.75 J/cm², giving roughly 2.5 µm of oxide. Curvature comes from geometry instead of grinding: 6 µm holes are opened in photoresist, the substrate is offset from the ablation target and rotated during growth, and the film shadows itself into a dome with an aspect ratio near one.

Under the lenses, saturation count rate rises on average 63% to 160 kc/s against 96–98 kc/s on bare diamond, and the optical power needed to saturate falls 33%, from 3.6 mW to 2.5 mW.

Two limits the authors name themselves: photolithographic placement is good only to 500–1000 nm laterally, and higher-index lenses are the more sensitive to geometry error, so the index you want and the alignment you can afford pull against each other. 'Fencing' — stray deposit on the resist sidewalls — also appears, with an effect they have not quantified. A separate line argues the structure is avoidable altogether: Weinbrenner and colleagues report saturation rates above 2.5 × 10⁵ counts per second from a bare interface collected from the back through oil immersion.

glossary.definition: A nitrogen atom sitting next to a missing carbon in diamond; it emits single photons and its spin state can be read optically, which is what makes it a nanoscale magnetometer.
A hemisphere of high-index material centred on an emitter so that rays cross its exit surface along a radius, which removes both refraction and total internal reflection at that surface.
Film growth in which a focused laser ablates a solid target and the plume condenses on a nearby substrate, carrying complex oxide stoichiometry across without heating the substrate.
Detected photons per second in thousands; the saturation value is the collection figure of merit because it is what the count rate approaches however hard you pump the emitter.

items.fab_angle: Shadowing a film into a dome through a resist hole by offsetting and rotating the substrate is a trick a sputter tool can do as well as a PLD chamber, and it needs no grey-scale mask or reflow. It is a realistic way for a teaching cleanroom to make a curved optic.

items.title: A stray quantum dot nobody designed turns out to be the better charge sensor
items.dek: M. R. Tanvir, Giordano Scappucci and Joseph Salfi read the charge state of a germanium quantum dot — a handful of mobile holes trapped under a metal gate — through that same gate at 540 megahertz, and found an unintended second dot left behind by fabrication lifted the signal-to-noise ratio about twentyfold.
items.why_it_matters: A dedicated detector costs an entire extra dot with its own two ohmic contacts, its own gates and its own wire to the outside, next to every qubit, and that overhead is what caps array density. Sensing through the gate deletes it. The accidental dot then shows the sensitivity lost that way can be recovered capacitively, by a charge island that carries no current at all.
items.background_md: A spin qubit in a semiconductor is never measured directly. The spin state is first converted into a charge configuration, and then something has to detect whether a single charge moved from one dot to its neighbour. The usual detector is a second quantum dot biased to pass current, whose conductance swings when the charge next door moves: accurate, but it needs its own ohmic contacts, its own gate set and its own line out of the fridge, and in a dense array that overhead scales with the qubit count. The alternative is to watch a gate's own impedance change as charge tunnels under it.
items.deeper_md:
The gate is made one arm of a resonator: 350 nH against about 0.25 pF resonating at 540 MHz with Q ≈ 100, giving a reflection dip near 30 dB when the device presents the matching resistance R = L/CZ₀ ≈ 30 kΩ. Read directly, the interdot transition of the few-hole double dot gives a power-SNR of 18.5 ± 3 in 50 ms of integration, reaching SNR 1 at about 2.7 ms. Routed through an unintentional single-hole box that happens to couple to one barrier gate, the same transition gives 372 ± 12, with SNR 1 at about 135 µs. The mechanism is that the interdot hop changes the Coulomb energy of the box more than it changes the double dot's own quantum capacitance, so a capacitive lever replaces a direct measurement.

Device: strained Ge quantum well about 55 nm below the surface, two Ti/Pd gate layers separated by 10 nm of Al₂O₃ plus 15 nm of ALD oxide, interdot tunnel coupling tc ≈ 5.37 ± 0.82 GHz.

The caveat is the dielectric. The authors attribute the ceiling to loss, not to amplifier noise: the matching resistance implies real loss even at 10 mK, the box signal falls sevenfold between 10 mK and 300 mK, and the optimum drive is only −95 dBm at the sample because more power degrades the match further. Candidate loss sources they list are Al₂O₃ defects, interface defects near the well, activated conduction in the well itself, and defects in the strain-relaxation buffer — none yet separated.

glossary.definition: The extra capacitance a gate sees because charge can tunnel on and off a dot in response to the gate's own RF voltage; it is the signal in gate-based readout and it is very small.
Signal power divided by noise power at the output of the reflectometry chain for a stated integration time; SNR 1 is the point at which one shot is barely conclusive.

A resonator only couples power efficiently into a device whose resistance equals L/CZ₀ against the 50 Ω line, so loss in the gate dielectric moves the circuit off match and directly costs sensitivity.
A quantum dot connected to just one reservoir, so charge moves in and out but never through; having no current path, it needs no ohmic contacts and adds almost no wiring.

items.fab_angle: The limiting number in this experiment is loss in 10 nm of ALD alumina and in the strain-relaxation buffer under the well, not in the amplifier. That makes gate-dielectric quality a readout spec rather than a leakage spec, which is a different thing to ask a process for.

items.title: Bit width sets the tile shape, so a bigger systolic array quantises harder
items.dek: Mikolaj Walczak and Tinoosh Mohsenin built a transformer accelerator in which different blocks of one weight matrix are held at 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits, each precision reusing the same multiplier grid over a different number of clock cycles, synthesised in a TSMC 16-nanometre kit at 2.8 trillion operations per watt.
items.why_it_matters: Bit widths are normally assigned one per tensor because the arithmetic hardware cannot do better than that. Letting them vary inside a tensor is only free if the array's geometry cooperates, and it stops cooperating as the array grows: the smallest group that can be given its own precision is tied to the array's side length, so scaling up pushes more weights to the coarsest levels and costs accuracy for reasons the quantisation algorithm never sees.
items.background_md: Inference hardware wants the fewest bits per weight that still answer correctly, because a narrower multiplier is a smaller and lower-energy circuit. Sensitivity is not spread evenly through a trained network: a few weight regions dominate the output and most are close to noise, which is the whole reason mixed-precision quantisation exists. The obstacle sits in the silicon rather than the algorithm. A systolic array — the grid of multiply-accumulate cells that marches operands past one another so each fetched value is reused many times — is wired for one operand width, and the array's own dimensions fix the smallest block that can be given a precision of its own.
items.deeper_md:
The coupling is explicit. At 8 bits each weight feeds one output column; at 4 bits two weights share the same input stream and produce two output columns over two cycles; 2-bit and 1-bit extend that to four and eight. Block height therefore scales as 8 divided by the precision, and the block is the unit precision is assigned to, which is how a p×p array's side length becomes a limit on granularity. Assignment itself is statistical: superblocks are ranked by standard deviation against cumulative-distribution cutoffs, with a per-layer relative variance score used for the diffusion model.

The 32×32 configuration in the TSMC 16 nm PDK at 1 GHz comes to 1.9 mm², 521 mW, 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/mm² and 2.8 TOPS/W, with 1666.2 KiB of on-chip SRAM.

Two numbers undercut the architecture and the authors report both. On-chip buffers are 86% of area at 4×4 and 79% at 32×32, so shrinking the multiplier array buys little of the die back. And the granularity penalty is real: DeiT-Small lands at 78.2% top-1 at a 4-bit effective width against an 81.2% baseline, and PixelDiT's gFID degrades from 14 at a 4×4 configuration to 50 at 16×16. Against the best published mixed-precision methods they are within 3.3% of accuracy at two bits lower effective width — which is the trade, not a free lunch, and a software-only scheme pays no array-geometry tax at all.

glossary.definition: A p×p grid of multiply-accumulate cells in which operands step from cell to cell every cycle, so each value read from memory is reused p times instead of being fetched again.
Trillions of integer operations per second per watt, the energy figure of merit for an inference accelerator; it is only meaningful alongside the clock and the operand precision it was measured at.
The average bits per weight once a mixed assignment is averaged over a tensor, so a 4-bit effective width here means the mixture of 1-, 2-, 4- and 8-bit blocks averages four.
Generative Fréchet inception distance, lower being better; it measures how far a generated image distribution sits from the real one and stands in for accuracy on the diffusion model.

items.fab_angle: The area split is the transferable lesson for anyone laying out an accelerator: with buffers at 79–86% of the die, arithmetic cleverness is a second-order lever and the SRAM floorplan is the first-order one.

items.title: In integer inference the rounding offsets matter more than multiplier width
items.dek: Yike Li and Deepu John released an open-source RISC-V inference platform that isolates the fixed-point rescaling after every integer convolution — the multiply-and-shift that brings a 32-bit accumulator back to 8 bits — and their ablation ranks its rounding offsets above the width of the multiplier doing the work.
items.why_it_matters: Hardware teams treat that rescaling as plumbing and approximate it wherever it saves cells, as though all the approximations were interchangeable. They are not: dropping the shift-stage offset moves accuracy most, because that offset is what stops truncation from biasing every output channel in the same direction, while the expensive change — widening the multiplier from 16 to 32 bits — is what costs 150% more DSP blocks.
items.background_md: Integer-only inference has one specific arithmetic shape. Weights and activations are 8-bit integers each carrying a scale factor, the multiply-accumulate runs into a 32-bit accumulator, and the result must then be brought back to 8 bits by multiplying by a real number: the input and weight scales divided by the output scale. Hardware cannot multiply by a real number, so that factor is stored as a fixed-point integer followed by a bit shift. Every design decision about how that step rounds is paid once per output element, which is why it is the arithmetic the whole scheme stands on.
items.deeper_md:
The pipeline the platform exposes is two stages. First `Qm = (ACC × Mi16 + round_m) >> 15`, where the real multiplier is scaled by 2¹⁵ and stored as a signed 16-bit integer and `round_m` is 2¹⁴ for non-negative products and 1 − 2¹⁴ for negative ones. Then `Qs = (Qm + round_s) >> Nc`, with a per-channel shift. The ablation cuts five variants — an int32 multiplier in place of int16, a shift shared across channels with multipliers rescaled to compensate, `round_m` removed, `round_s` removed, and both removed — and finds removal of the shift rounding produces substantially larger deviations than any other.

The platform is a VexRiscv control core driving accelerator cores of four pcores with eight ALU lanes each, on a Digilent Arty A7-100T at 83.3 MHz. Cost of full fidelity: 47,126 slice LUTs (+26.3%), 52,084 registers (+12.6%) and 160 DSPs (+150%), with block RAM unchanged. Accuracy against TensorFlow Lite stays inside 0.25 percentage points on every model tested — LeNet-5 at 99.19% top-1, SqueezeNet1.1 at 57.72% (−0.23 pp), MobileNetV1 at 68.95% (0 pp), MobileNetV2 at 71.10% in UINT8 (−0.02 pp), ResNet-18 at 69.50% (−0.07 pp), ResNet-50 at 74.36% (−0.22 pp).

Nobody disputes the arithmetic; the open question is reach. These are Artix-7 fabric counts, not ASIC area, and the DSP figure partly reflects how Xilinx multiply blocks pack a 32-bit product rather than a general cost. The ablation is also convolutional networks only, so the ranking is untested on attention layers.

glossary.definition: The multiply-and-shift that converts a wide accumulator back to 8 bits using the ratio of input, weight and output scale factors; it is the only place a real number enters an integer-only pipeline.
The unit for a difference between two accuracies: 74.58% down to 74.36% is 0.22 pp, which is not the same quantity as a 0.22% relative change.
The hard multiply-accumulate unit built into FPGA fabric; a 32-bit product needs several cascaded where a 16-bit product needs one, which is where this design's 150% overhead comes from.
A constant added before a right shift so that truncation rounds to nearest rather than always toward zero, which keeps the shift from biasing a channel's outputs in one direction.

items.title: Make the e-graph store multisets and the commutativity explosion stops
items.dek: Tarik Rosin, Marcel Ullrich and Sebastian Hack showed that an optimiser which rewrites a program by keeping every equivalent form at once grows to roughly 3ⁿ stored terms on addition and multiplication alone, and that holding those operands as unordered multisets removes most of the growth.
items.why_it_matters: The appeal of this technique is that it never commits to a rewrite order, so an early simplification cannot destroy the shape a later rule needed. Associativity and commutativity are the two rules every arithmetic rule set must have and the two that make the structure unaffordable, which means the practical ceiling on expression size has been set by bookkeeping rather than by the optimisation being attempted.
items.background_md: A compiler applying rewrite rules one at a time has to pick an order, and the pick is often wrong: simplifying early can remove the pattern a later rule needed. Equality saturation avoids choosing. It builds an e-graph, a structure holding equivalence classes of expressions, applies every rule everywhere until nothing new appears, and only then extracts the cheapest member of the class containing the original program. The price is that the graph grows with every form it remembers, and for some rule sets the growth has no fixed point at all.
items.deeper_md:
The blow-up is countable. For a term over n distinct variables, an AC-saturated e-graph holds 2ⁿ − 1 e-classes, one per non-empty subset of the variables, and 3ⁿ − 2ⁿ⁺¹ + n + 1 e-nodes. Worse, saturation need not exist: the paper's opening example pairs x·0 = 0 with associativity, and a·0 generates a·(a·0), which generates (a·a)·0, forever.

The fix is representational. An AC operator is flattened into a multiset of operands, so every AC-equivalent spelling of a term shares one e-node, and nodes are split into explicit ones stored as tuples and implicit ones that exist only as sub-multisets of an explicit node, so only a fraction consume memory. Their asymptotic table: a repeated-variable sum x₁+…+x₁ falls from O(n²) e-nodes to O(1), a distinct-variable sum from O(2ⁿ) to O(n), and wrapping either in a homomorphism h(x₁+…+xₙ) leaves both at O(2ⁿ). Measured against egg: h(abc) needs 42 e-nodes versus 14, and a·b·a⁻¹·b⁻¹ needs 55 versus 11.

The authors state the cost honestly. Their matching is incomplete, because a pattern variable can bind to one e-class id but not to a subset of them, so a + b + −(a+b) is not matched once the sum has been flattened; they say more work is needed to judge how much that loses. The worst case is still exponential memory, and the results are labelled preliminary.

glossary.definition: A graph storing sets of expressions grouped into equivalence classes, so a single node can stand for every form the tool has proved equal — the structure that lets a rewriter avoid choosing an order.
Operators like + and × where neither grouping nor order changes the value, so a sum of n terms has exponentially many spellings that a naive rewriter stores separately.
Finding every place in an e-graph where a rule's left-hand side applies. It dominates the cost of equality saturation, and the relational formulation treats it as a database join.
The point at which applying every rule yields no new nodes. Some rule sets never reach it, which is why real implementations also impose node-count and time limits.

items.title: A linearizable read that is cheap for the reader is expensive for the writer
items.dek: Aleksey Panas mapped the design space for reads in a replicated datastore that must never hand back a stale value, and showed the choices collapse onto one dial: every round trip a reader saves has to be paid for by the writer waiting on more replicas.
items.why_it_matters: Implementations pick a point on that dial at build time — Raft offers a leader lease or a commit-index exchange, Paxos Quorum Reads offers a follower quorum — and which point is right depends on which link happens to be slow this week. Turning the choice into a runtime reconfiguration lets a cluster route around a replica that has gone slow instead of inheriting its latency.
items.background_md: Replicated storage keeps the same data on several machines so that one can fail without losing it. Linearizability is the strongest promise such a system can make: every read returns the value of the most recently completed write, as though there were a single copy. It is hard because a write is only committed once a majority has acknowledged it, so a replica that has not heard yet still holds the old value, and a reader who asks only that replica is handed it. Every standard fix adds communication somewhere; the design question is whose latency pays.
items.deeper_md:
The taxonomy has two axes: how a read handles a write it may have caught mid-flight — invalidation, eager stamping or delayed stamping — and the read-write quorum system, from a local read of one process up to a majority. Two consequences follow. Shrinking read quorums to cut read latency forces write quorums to grow, because a write must reach a majority *and* intersect every read quorum. And at a fixed read quorum size, larger quorums let a leader route around a slow process, whereas a single-process local reader pins every write to that one process.

Ditto keeps the quorum configuration in a separate linearizable configuration layer and, on any change, fetches the leader's latest prepare index and enforces it as a floor on later reads, so a new quorum cannot miss a write committed under the old one.

The evaluation is a 7-process line topology on symmetric 50 ms links. Write latency floors near 300 ms because of the majority requirement, and delayed stamping takes the leader's worst-case read from roughly 300 ms to roughly 0 ms and a distant node's from about 400 ms to about 200 ms; a fail-slow variant adds 3000 ms to two processes' incoming links. Caveats: leases need bounded clock drift and generate renewal traffic, read throughput is not addressed, and the reconfiguration policy — when to actually move the dial — is left to future work, which is the part an operator needs. Single-author preprint, no venue.

glossary.definition: The guarantee that every operation appears to take effect at one instant between its call and its return, so a read never returns a value older than an already-completed write.
The set of replicas an operation must hear from. Correctness needs every read quorum to intersect every write quorum, which is exactly why shrinking one forces the other to grow.
A replica still answering but far later than it should. It is harder to handle than an outright crash, because failure detectors do not fire and the system keeps waiting on it.
Attaching a log index to a read so the reader can tell whether a write it glimpsed is committed; eager stamping settles that before returning, delayed stamping defers it.

items.title: Replicate the hot expert at run time and ship its weights while it computes
items.dek: Jianzhu Yao and Christos Kozyrakis built MegaFlux, which decides inside a mixture-of-experts layer which overloaded experts to duplicate onto idle GPUs and overlaps copying those experts' weights with the arithmetic that consumes them, for 1.45× the forward speed of fixed placement on eight Nvidia B200s.
items.why_it_matters: When a router sends uneven numbers of tokens to experts spread across GPUs, one GPU finishes last and sets the whole layer's latency while the rest idle, and tuning placement offline cannot track a distribution that changes with the prompt. Making replication a decision inside the kernel turns the weight transfer it requires into a pipeline stage instead of a serial tax, and that transfer cost is what decides whether replicating is worth doing.
items.background_md: A mixture-of-experts layer holds many feed-forward blocks and routes each token to only a few of them, so parameter count can grow without the arithmetic per token growing with it. Once those blocks live on different GPUs, every token has to be sent to wherever its expert sits and the result sent back — an all-to-all exchange twice per layer. An all-to-all is only as fast as its slowest participant, and a router free to send tokens wherever it likes does not spread them evenly, so some GPUs are handed several times their share.
items.deeper_md:
A megakernel fuses the expert-parallel communication with the expert computation, so there is no kernel boundary between moving a token and using it. MegaFlux adds an on-device planner that chooses replica locations and assigns tile-aligned token blocks under a per-GPU replica budget, leaving the router's own outputs untouched, so model behaviour is unchanged. Replicas begin computing as their weights arrive; the backward pass overlaps replica-gradient reduction with ongoing expert computation.

Across 147 configurations per direction on eight Nvidia B200 GPUs, the geometric-mean gain over the same megakernels with fixed placement is 1.45× forward and 1.28× backward, peaking at 2.14× and 2.64×. Pipelining is what pays for it: it hides 56–76% of the replica weight-transfer cost in the forward pass and 91–100% of the combined transfer and gradient-reduction cost in the backward pass, worth a further 13.2% and 26.7% of layer latency against running the same replication plans as separate steps.

The honest number is the smallest one. Integrated into vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Pro prefill, end-to-end median speedup is 1.13–1.26×, well under the kernel-level figure, because a layer is not a model. The baseline is the authors' own fixed-placement megakernel built on TensorRT-LLM's CuTeDSL MoE forward kernel rather than a weaker library, which strengthens the comparison, but it is still their own harness. And replication spends HBM capacity, bounded only by the replica budget, which is the one resource a large MoE deployment is already short of.

glossary.definition: A layer of many parallel feed-forward blocks where a learned router sends each token to only a few, so parameter count rises while the arithmetic done per token does not.
One GPU kernel that fuses what would otherwise be several launches — here communication and expert computation — so data can move and be consumed without returning to the host scheduler.
The uneven spread of tokens across experts, which leaves one GPU holding the most work; since the layer cannot finish until that GPU does, its latency becomes the layer's latency.
The n-th root of the product of n ratios, used instead of an average because speedups multiply; it sits below the arithmetic mean and is harder to inflate with a single outlier.

foundations.subtitle: The 1964 machine that split what a program can see from how the hardware does it, and turned the first half into a contract.
foundations.tldr: Before 1964 a faster computer meant rewriting your programs, because each machine's instruction set was a description of its own wiring. IBM's System/360 wrote the instruction set down first and then built six machines with wildly different insides that all obeyed it, spending microcode to make slow narrow hardware imitate the behaviour of fast wide hardware. That separation — architecture as a published contract, implementation as the manufacturer's problem — is now how every processor family works, and parts of the 1964 contract are still enforced in IBM's current mainframes.

sections.heading: Every new computer meant rewriting every program
sections.body_md: In the early 1960s a computer's instruction set was an accident of its hardware. IBM alone sold several incompatible lines, and a customer outgrowing one machine had to discard the programs written for it and start again, because the next machine up had different registers, different data formats and different input/output. That is a tax on success: the better the business did, the more software it destroyed. System/360, announced on 7 April 1964, was the answer, and IBM's own account of it calls the programme a five-billion-dollar gamble spread over four years — a figure worth noting mainly because it tells you the company understood it was betting on an idea rather than on a machine. The announcement covered six processor models spanning a fiftyfold range of performance plus fifty-four peripheral devices, and the claim attached to it is the part that mattered: software written for one model would run on any other model in the line.
sections.deeper_md: Two of the six announced models, the 60 and 62, were never shipped, which is a useful reminder that the line as announced and the line as delivered were not the same thing. The compatibility claim also had an exception at the bottom: the Model 20, positioned below the Model 30, was not fully compatible with the family it was sold into. Counting it in stretches the performance spread of the eventual range to roughly 3000:1 between the Model 20 and the later Model 195.

sections.heading: Architecture became a separate noun
sections.body_md: The idea underneath is a boundary drawn on purpose. Write down everything a program can observe — the instructions, the registers, the data formats, how storage is addressed, what happens on an interrupt — and call that the architecture. Everything else, how wide the adder is, how many cycles a multiply takes, whether there is a cache, is implementation, and the manufacturer may change it freely. Before 1964 the two were one document, because the instruction set was simply a readable description of the wiring. Separating them turns the architecture into a contract with two signatures. The programmer promises to rely only on what is written down. The manufacturer promises that anything written down will keep working on hardware that does not exist yet, built by engineers who have not been hired yet. Every processor family since is a restatement of that deal, and every argument about whether some behaviour is a bug or a feature is an argument about where the line was drawn.

sections.heading: One instruction set, six different machines underneath
sections.body_md: The proof that the boundary was real is how little the models shared internally. The Model 30 near the bottom had an eight-bit data bus and an eight-bit arithmetic unit, so a 32-bit addition took it four passes. The Model 50 in the middle moved 32 bits at a time, with a separate eight-bit path called the mover for byte work. The Model 65 above it used a 64-bit bus and several specialised adders. All three executed the same instructions and produced the same answers, which is only possible because an instruction had been defined by its result rather than by its mechanism. Storage spread the same way: the Model 20 shipped with four to thirty-two kilobytes of core, the Model 30 with eight to sixty-four. The original line's slowest and fastest members differed roughly fiftyfold in throughput, and a program could not tell which one it was running on.

sections.heading: Microcode is what made the family affordable
sections.body_md: Building six machines that imitate one behaviour would be hopeless if each had to implement every instruction in hard-wired logic, because the complicated instructions dominate the design effort and the cheap machines could never pay for them. IBM's answer was to make the cheap machines interpreters. Inside each processor sat a read-only control store holding microinstructions — very wide, very simple commands that open gates, step the adder, move a byte — and the System/360 instruction set was implemented as programs written in that store. The Model 50's microinstruction is 90 bits wide and divided into 28 separate fields, each steering a different piece of the datapath in the same cycle, and its control store holds 2,816 such words. The economics are the whole point: a microcoded machine pays a roughly fixed cost for the interpreter and only a small increment for each additional instruction, so a long instruction list stops being a luxury good.
sections.deeper_md: This is why microcode and the compatible family arrived together rather than by coincidence. Hard-wired control makes the cost of an instruction set roughly proportional to its size, which forces cheap machines to have small instruction sets, which makes a compatible family impossible. Interpretation breaks that link by trading cycles for logic — the Model 30 spends four passes on a 32-bit addition the Model 50 does in one — and cycles are exactly what a customer buying the cheapest model has already agreed to spend. The published figure that makes the argument is the one about overhead: a microcoded design carries a roughly fixed cost and only a small increment per extra instruction.

sections.heading: A read-only memory, built four different ways
sections.body_md: None of that was easy in 1964, because semiconductor memory did not exist as a product and the control store had to be faster than main core storage while costing almost nothing. The low end used CCROS, a card capacitive read-only store: microinstructions were punched into metallised Mylar cards on an ordinary keypunch and read out as a matrix of capacitors. The Model 30 carried 42 boards of eight cards each, 4,032 words of 60 bits. The Model 20 and Model 40 used TROS instead, a stack of Mylar sheets whose drive lines either thread through a transformer core, read as a one, or pass around it, read as a zero — 15,360 bits, or 1,920 bytes, per module. The Model 50 used BCROS, two etched copper squares per bit on sheets 20 by 8½ inches. Three storage technologies, one architecture: precisely the substitution the contract was written to allow.
sections.deeper_md: Notice what the choice of control store is doing. It is not a performance tier chosen for its own sake; it is whatever hits each model's required microinstruction access time at that model's price. CCROS is the cheap end, and its cards are punched on an ordinary keypunch, so a correction is a punching job rather than a fabrication job. BCROS is explicitly the faster of the two and needs an etched copper laminate. All of them are invisible above the line, which means IBM could change them between models without telling a single programmer — and what let it do so was having written down in advance what a programmer is entitled to observe.

sections.heading: The contract outlived the hardware, and it still binds
sections.body_md: System/360 addresses were 24 bits, which gave each program sixteen megabytes. That was generous in 1964 and a problem by the late 1970s, and what IBM did next is the real test of the idea. It extended addressing to 31 bits, taking an address space to two gigabytes, and later to 64 bits — and in both cases kept the older mode rather than retiring it. A current mainframe therefore has three addressing modes, selected by bits in the program status word, with instructions named SAM24, SAM31 and SAM64 to switch between them and a Test Addressing Mode instruction whose condition code reads 0 for 24-bit and 3 for 64-bit. IBM's own documentation states plainly that the extension did not require customers to change existing programs. Code written against the 1964 contract can still ask the machine which world it is in. That is what a contract costs, and it is also what one is worth.

glossary.definition: The set of things a program can observe — instructions, registers, data formats, addressing, interrupt behaviour — that the manufacturer promises not to change. Everything else about the hardware is implementation and may change without notice.

A program held inside the processor, in control storage, that implements each machine instruction as a sequence of very wide low-level steps. It is what lets slow, narrow hardware imitate the behaviour of fast, wide hardware.

One word of microcode. The Model 50's is 90 bits wide and split into 28 fields, each steering a different part of the datapath in the same clock — wide rather than dense, because it is control signals and not encoded operations.

The read-only memory holding microcode. System/360 used metallised punched cards read capacitively, Mylar sheets threaded through transformer cores, and pairs of etched copper capacitors, depending on each model's required speed and price.

How many bits of an address the processor treats as significant: 24 bits reach 16 MB, 31 bits reach 2 GB, 64 bits reach 16 EB. A mainframe can switch between all three at run time with SAM24, SAM31 and SAM64.

The eight-bit addressable unit System/360 popularised. Making storage byte-addressable rather than word-addressable is what let character data and binary arithmetic live comfortably on the same machine.

foundations.try_this: Open the Model 50 microcode write-up cited below, find the field map of the 90-bit microinstruction, pick one field and work out what would stop working if it were deleted — that is the fastest way to feel the difference between control signals and instructions. Then do the same job for MNF's own chip. Write the one page that says what the IC must do: pin behaviour, register map, the timing you intend to hold fixed. Date it, and put it under version control before anyone places a cell. Everything not on that page is implementation and you are free to change it; the useful shock of the exercise is discovering how much of what the team calls the design is actually implementation nobody agreed to freeze.
